title: Scientists May Have Found a Lost Roman City in Austria
summary:
Along the Danube River in Austria, researchers may have found an entire Roman city lost for nearly 2,000 years. The area was part of the Danube Limes, the Roman Empire's frontier along the river, part of which is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Since 2015, a team from several fields has studied a roughly six-mile stretch of frontier between the towns of Enns and St. Pantaleon-Erla, in what was once the northern border of the Roman province of Noricum.

Geophysical surveys revealed a previously unknown city near the hamlet of Stein. It covered about 62 to 74 acres and was carefully planned, with a grid of streets like a modern city's. Its most impressive feature was an amphitheater that could seat about 8,000 spectators. The city appears to have been founded next to a military garrison around 80 C.E. and abandoned about a century later. Researchers found no signs of destruction, so residents probably left in an orderly way.

Could this be Claudivium, a city mentioned by second-century geographer Claudius Ptolemy? The new site fits the coordinates Ptolemy gave, and a river he described flowing in from the north could be the Aist, which joins the Danube nearby. The name Claudivium also disappears from historical records after about 180 C.E., around when this city was abandoned.

Over three years, archaeologist Mario Wallner of GeoSphere Austria and colleagues scanned the site with ground-penetrating radar and magnetometry, mapping buried roads that cannot be seen from the surface. About 640 coins have been recovered, and a large cemetery lies to the northwest.

Why leave a thriving city? After Emperor Marcus Aurelius died in 180 C.E., his son Commodus signed a peace treaty ending the Marcomannic Wars. Rome then reorganized its frontier defenses, concentrated forces at nearby Lauriacum, and gave up the settlement at Stein. Similar tools and clothing pins found at Lauriacum suggest craftspeople moved there. The identification remains uncertain, however, because no inscription bearing the name Claudivium has been found.
why_it_matters: Finding a whole planned city helps historians understand how Rome defended and organised its frontier. It also shows how scanning tools can reveal buried history without disturbing the ground.

background_read: The Danube Limes was the Roman Empire's frontier along the Danube River, guarding the northern border of provinces such as Noricum.
Roman frontier settlements often grew up next to a military garrison and were carefully planned, with streets laid out in a grid.
Archaeologists can study buried cities without digging them up by scanning the ground with tools such as ground-penetrating radar and magnetometry.
A second-century geographer named Claudius Ptolemy mentioned a city called Claudivium, and researchers are testing whether this newly mapped site could be that lost city.
